title: Why Do Some Nuclei Grow? The Critical Radius

speech_units.raw_text: Why do some tiny crystal nuclei disappear, while others keep growing? The answer is energy competition.
speech_units.display_text: Why do some tiny crystal nuclei disappear, while others keep growing? The answer is energy competition.
speech_units.spoken_text: Why do some tiny crystal nuclei disappear, while others keep growing? The answer is energy competition.

speech_units.raw_text: Classical homogeneous nucleation theory describes a spherical nucleus using two terms: a positive surface cost and a negative bulk contribution.
speech_units.display_text: Classical homogeneous nucleation theory describes a spherical nucleus using two terms: a positive surface cost and a negative bulk contribution.
speech_units.spoken_text: Classical homogeneous nucleation theory describes a spherical nucleus using two terms: a positive surface cost and a negative bulk contribution.

speech_units.raw_text: The surface cost scales with area, or radius squared. The bulk contribution scales with volume, or radius cubed.
speech_units.display_text: The surface cost scales with area, or radius squared. The bulk contribution scales with volume, or radius cubed.
speech_units.spoken_text: The surface cost scales with area, or radius squared. The bulk contribution scales with volume, or radius cubed.

speech_units.raw_text: At small sizes, surface cost dominates, so total free energy rises. As the nucleus grows, bulk gain becomes stronger.
speech_units.display_text: At small sizes, surface cost dominates, so total free energy rises. As the nucleus grows, bulk gain becomes stronger.
speech_units.spoken_text: At small sizes, surface cost dominates, so total free energy rises. As the nucleus grows, bulk gain becomes stronger.

speech_units.raw_text: The free-energy curve reaches a maximum at the critical radius. Below it, shrinking is favored; above it, growth lowers free energy.
speech_units.display_text: The free-energy curve reaches a maximum at the critical radius. Below it, shrinking is favored; above it, growth lowers free energy.
speech_units.spoken_text: The free-energy curve reaches a maximum at the critical radius. Below it, shrinking is favored; above it, growth lowers free energy.

speech_units.raw_text: The critical radius equals two gamma divided by the bulk driving-force magnitude.
speech_units.display_text: The critical radius equals two gamma divided by the bulk driving-force magnitude.
speech_units.spoken_text: The critical radius equals two gamma divided by the bulk driving-force magnitude.

speech_units.raw_text: The barrier height scales with interfacial energy cubed and inversely with the driving force squared.
speech_units.display_text: The barrier height scales with interfacial energy cubed and inversely with the driving force squared.
speech_units.spoken_text: The barrier height scales with interfacial energy cubed and inversely with the driving force squared.

speech_units.raw_text: This model assumes homogeneous nucleation, a spherical nucleus, and an isotropic interface. Real systems also depend on interface structure, anisotropy, transport, and kinetics.
speech_units.display_text: This model assumes homogeneous nucleation, a spherical nucleus, and an isotropic interface. Real systems also depend on interface structure, anisotropy, transport, and kinetics.
speech_units.spoken_text: This model assumes homogeneous nucleation, a spherical nucleus, and an isotropic interface. Real systems also depend on interface structure, anisotropy, transport, and kinetics.
